November 1, 2026

The Local AI Opportunity

Why AI will diffuse through society as a GPU per person

@iamgingertrash

Every era of computing has had its own way of running the meter. On a mainframe, you bought time: a few minutes on an expensive machine that belonged to somebody else. The internet made us familiar with bandwidth. We learned to think of a connection as a pipe, and paid for a wider one when we wanted more to flow through it. Now we are learning to count tokens, the little pieces of language a model reads and produces as it works.

As tokens get cheaper, we can afford to give the machine jobs that would once have seemed extravagant. Something similar happened when Britain learned to get more work out of a ton of coal. A more efficient steam engine saved its owner fuel, but it also made steam power affordable to the next factory owner, who had previously done without. Multiply that decision across an industrializing country and the coal saved by individual engines was overtaken by the coal burned in new ones. William Stanley Jevons described the result in 1865:

“It is wholly a confusion of ideas to suppose that the economical use of fuel is equivalent to a diminished consumption. The very contrary is the truth.”W. Stanley Jevons, The Coal Question, 1865

Since ChatGPT arrived, we have kept spending the savings on more ambitious requests. A question that once seemed worth a short answer becomes worth an afternoon of research; a useful coding suggestion makes us wonder whether the model could build the whole thing. As these jobs become affordable and reliable, they enter the routine, and our idea of normal use expands to include them.

2023 · Chatbots

The first chatbots answered simple questions:

What is the capital of France?
Paris is the capital of France.
How many ounces are in a pound?
There are 16 ounces in a pound.

Each exchange cost a few dozen tokens, and a whole day of use rarely crossed 100.

2025 · Early agents

Then came short-horizon agents that could do small jobs on their own, like answering email, browsing the web, or running a piece of research for you:

Who are the 5 biggest home-battery makers, and how do their prices compare?
web.search(“biggest home battery manufacturers”) browser.read(14 pages) docs.extract(spec_sheets: Tesla, BYD, LG, Enphase, Sonnen) calc.normalize(“$ / kWh installed”) → Powerwall 3 ≈ $1,000/kWh; BYD undercuts it at… truncated

One of these chats ran to 5,000 tokens or more, and nobody minded, because the work was worth it.

2026–27 · Strong agents

Now there are strong agents that carry a long task from start to finish, building a piece of software end to end or reverse-engineering an app, in runs that last tens of hours:

Port our billing service off the legacy API and migrate the tests.
repo.read(212 files) code.map(“legacy_api.*”) → 47 call sites code.rewrite(“billing/client.ts”) tests.run() → 14 failures tests.run() → pass webhooks.migrate() — day 2… truncated

A run like that burns 100,000 tokens without trying, and the number climbs with every improvement in memory, context, and tool use, because each one makes a longer run worth paying for.

2027½ and beyond · Always-on

The last step is the loop that never closes: an agent that is never prompted and never stops.

New information is just another injection into its stream of tokens, and it runs all day and all night on behalf of 1 human. The first of these are already here, in Grok Bot, Instinct, Muse, and Dot. The curve goes vertical when they become ordinary.

We keep finding more work for AI, but supplying the tokens is becoming the harder problem. A more capable agent gives millions of people a reason to ask more of it, and that extra demand can arrive with a software update.

Those extra tokens, however, still have to come from machines running in datacenters.

Expanding those facilities means securing electricity, land, and permission to build, which can take years. The chart shows the opportunity created when demand for tokens pulls sharply away from the cloud’s capacity to supply them.1

Even if energy, land, and regulation were no obstacle, there would still be no obvious ceiling on the work we could find for intelligence. This creates a situation I described to some of my investors in May:

The Agentic Paradox

The better an agent becomes, the longer it is worth keeping it at work. Better memory and tool use can increase its consumption even without making the model larger. If the model also requires more computation per token, we are asking each machine to do more work for each user while every user wants more of its time.

We think much of that unmet demand will eventually find its way onto a personal inference machine. A computer you buy and keep running, producing tokens throughout the day, with electricity as its main ongoing cost.

It is an incredibly unsexy idea at a time when sexy ideas command enormous premiums. But who really wants a computer you plug into the wall when you can have mass drivers on the Moon, or cover the Sahara with “intelligence factories,” the modern Mecca of AI psychosis victims?

A remarkably similar thing happened in the 1970s. Much of computing revolved around large machines owned by institutions, with users buying or being allocated time on them. The first personal computers looked unimpressive beside those installations. They had little memory, limited software, and owners who often had to work quite hard to make them useful.

But as the machines improved, someone who wanted to write a document or keep the accounts for a small business could increasingly do it on a computer of their own. Each useful new application gave another person a reason to buy one. Computing began spreading through purchases made by its users, into buildings that already existed, drawing on electricity already available there.

Suppose 1 billion people each have a personal agent that reads their messages, follows their work on screen, and uses their apps to get things done. For this calculation, assume each agent generates 50 tokens a second, continuously. Serving that workload from datacenters would require:

Tok/s required5 × 1010 tokens per second
Tokens per day≈ 4.3 quadrillion
H200 equivalents≈ 80,000,000 GPUs
Power at roughly 2 joules per token100 GW, continuous
Energy per year≈ 880 TWh
Cost to build≈ $3.5 trillion

100 gigawatts is roughly the generating capacity of the entire American nuclear fleet. Under our assumptions, personal agents would keep the equivalent of that fleet occupied around the clock, before accounting for model training or other uses of AI.

The natural response is to build more datacenters. I expect we will build a great many. What I doubt is that they will arrive fast enough to keep up with what we want from them. Approving a construction budget does not settle when the electricity will be available, or whether the community chosen to host the project wants it there. Those decisions belong to utility planners, neighbors, and elected officials, none of whom is obliged to share an AI company’s timetable.

The Three Caps

Not all things are built at the speed of bits

The Grid

A datacenter is, before anything else, a connection to the electric grid. Google now calls transmission the single biggest threat to its datacenter expansion, and in parts of the country the wait for a connection has passed 10 years.2 A 100-megawatt connection averages 7 years, and Berkeley Lab data show that the wait has doubled.3

These delays are not administrative accidents. They are the physical schedule of high-voltage construction: routing, permitting, transformer backlogs, eminent domain. Chips come out of a fab in months. A transmission line takes years, which is how you end up with GPUs sitting in warehouses, waiting for electricity that does not exist yet.

The Neighbors

Suppose the grid were solved. A datacenter is still a windowless box the size of several football fields that hums through the night and draws on the local water and power. People do not want one next door, and they have started to say so in ways that cost money. Data Center Watch counted $64B of American projects blocked or delayed by local opposition.4 By early 2026 the count had reached roughly $130B in a single quarter, with 833 opposition groups organized across 49 states, and the second quarter added 45 more projects worth $68B.5

And the opposition is not a fringe. In the poll above, 69% of voters oppose a datacenter in their own community, a majority of Democrats, Republicans, and independents alike, and a separate Annenberg survey puts the figure at 3 in 5.6

The State

Where the neighbors organize, the state eventually follows. In August 2026 Governor Greg Abbott halted datacenter grid approvals across Texas pending an audit,7 an order that froze 474 gigawatts of pending connection requests, more than 5 times the record peak demand of the entire ERCOT system.8 In September he extended the halt to every environmental permit a datacenter needs, and the audit is due in December. New York went further. Governor Hochul froze new hyperscale datacenters by executive order in July, the legislature passed a 1-year ban behind it, and nearly 2/3 of New Yorkers polled want the ban kept when it expires.9

Nor is this a passing mood in 2 statehouses. Wood Mackenzie counts more than 400 datacenter moratoriums enacted since January across 42 states, touching nearly 20% of the sites it tracks and more than 100 gigawatts of planned capacity, and the Texas pause alone puts 60 gigawatts of projects under audit.10

Then came the midterms. Going in, NBC found 64% of voters less likely to support a candidate who backed a local datacenter, and 11% more likely. On November 3 datacenters were on the ballot 41 times in 10 states, and the industry won once, in Harwood, North Dakota. Wells, Maine passed a retroactive 6-month moratorium with more than 80% of the vote. Of the 74 candidates for governor that Data Center Watch tracked, 43% had backed a moratorium or a ban, and that side won the statehouses that matter most. Texas, which holds about 25% of the datacenter capacity in the works, went to Gina Hinojosa on a promise to freeze approvals until the legislature writes rules; Ohio went to Amy Acton and Georgia to Keisha Lance Bottoms, who ran on the same issue. In the NBC exit poll, 56% of voters called AI and datacenters a major factor in their vote for Congress.10 The political price of saying yes to a datacenter is no longer rising. It has been paid, in public, by candidates who said yes, and nothing about the demand curve in Figure 1 will bring it back down.

So what’s the reality?

Against those 100 gigawatts, what is actually being built?

Goldman Sachs projects American datacenter additions of 13.6 GW in 2026 and 36.3 in 2027, the most optimistic reputable schedule in print.11

Jefferies puts the likely pace at 15–20 GW a year. Construction has begun on only 12 of the 24 GW planned for 2026, and as much as 80% of the 2027–28 pipeline has yet to break ground.12

Financing the buildout

The companies borrowing to build all this capacity also have to finance the wait. If a grid connection slips by a year, interest keeps accumulating while the revenue meant to repay the loan moves further away. With floating-rate debt, the interest bill can rise during the delay. September’s Fed rate increase added to that pressure.13

The internet boom also became a construction boom. Telecom companies borrowed heavily to lay fiber, and Greenspan’s Fed raised rates from 4.75 to 6.5% as the buildout approached its peak. When revenues disappointed and financing dried up, many of those companies went bankrupt, even as internet use kept growing.14

Today’s developers may have customers waiting for every machine they can install, but still have to survive the expense of getting those machines connected and earning money. In October, one of CoreWeave’s bonds briefly traded above a 16% yield.15 That suggests financing the next building could be considerably more expensive than financing the last one.

The cloud could have a very good decade and still fail to supply all the computing people want. Its datacenters could be full, its operators profitable, and the queue for capacity longer every year. That would be enough to create a substantial market for local inference, without any of the financial disasters discussed above.

Our model puts that shortfall at about $5 trillion by 2030, valued at the cloud prices it assumes.16 Serving the same workload locally would take roughly 550 million personal AI computers. These are computers people would buy because they have work for them, much as they once bought PCs to do work they could not conveniently do on a mainframe.

History seems to be repeating itself.

But before making the case for another generation of personal computers, we should examine the alternatives in depth. There are 3 proposals to consider:

  1. Just build more, bro.
  2. Put the datacenters in space.
  3. A GPU per person.

The next section gets into them.

The Three Paths

Cover the planet in datacenters, put them in space, or give every human their own GPU

Just Build More, Bro

The current era of AI was built in datacenters, so the default plan is more of what already works.

Here is how the US buildout compares with the plans, measured in total datacenter capacity:17

The May schedule called for 133 GW by the end of 2027. Goldman’s October forecast puts delivery at 90 GW, leaving a projected shortfall of 43 GW.

Part of the problem is that you can buy the computers long before you have somewhere to run them. The building still needs to be finished, the cooling installed, and the utility ready to supply the power. The chips can arrive while all of that is still being worked out.

Microsoft is already in this position. Satya Nadella has said its constraint is finding “warm shells” to put the chips in: buildings with the power and cooling needed to use them.

Tesla ran into the same problem. When 12,000 H100s meant for Tesla were redirected to X, Musk explained that they “would have just sat in the warehouse.” Tesla had ordered the computers before it had a datacenter ready for them.18

When Elon Musk himself is warning that power, cooling and electrical equipment could limit the buildout, you have to ask whether “just build more” is a viable plan in the first place.

Put Them Into Space

The second proposal is to put the datacenters in orbit. The attraction is easy to see: abundant sunlight, no land to buy, and no neighbors trying to stop you.

Serious teams are already working on this. Google’s Project Suncatcher plans to launch 2 prototype satellites carrying TPUs by early 2027.19 Starcloud, now valued at $2.3B, sent an Nvidia H100 into orbit in November 2025 and used it to train a small model on Shakespeare.20

But putting a computer in space also makes it harder to cool. There is no air to carry the heat away, so the satellite has to shed it as infrared radiation. The more power you give the computers, the more radiator area you need.

For a 100 MW datacenter, the estimate is roughly 500,000 square meters of radiators: thousands of tons of panels that also have to reach orbit. Radiators and solar arrays together account for about 2/3 of the satellite’s mass. Much of what you are launching is there just to supply the computers with electricity and get rid of the resulting heat.

You also lose the convenience of sending a technician over when something breaks. Getting equipment into orbit is expensive; returning to repair it is another undertaking. Google’s own analysis puts the launch cost needed to make the economics work below $200 per kilogram. Today’s price is about 14 times that.21

Starship would have to become a reliable, frequent way to move hardware into orbit, and launch prices would have to keep falling for years. Google’s projection reaches the necessary price in the mid-2030s.

We may eventually build datacenters in orbit, but the capacity we need in 2027 will have to come from somewhere else.

“Plurality must never be posited without necessity.”William of Ockham, c. 1320

A GPU Per Person

Ockham’s rule is useful here because these proposals ask us to solve very different problems.

More datacenters mean securing land, power and permission at every new site and orbit means making launches of an enormous rocket cheap and routine.

The third proposal is to sell people a computer with a GPU and the models already installed.

It's so simple, you almost hope it fails. Founders today focus on the sexiest, most outlandish ideas because the market awards enormous premiums to the biggest of claims.

By contrast, simple ideas are unsexy, and make us question everything we understand about progress. Surely history doesnt have the answers to all our problems. If it did, how could I, a 20-something year old tech founder possibly make my mark as the new Elon, Jobs, or DaVinci?

We have spent decades learning how to make computers affordable, manufacture millions of them, and ship them around the world, so let's do that again - with a new computer, one designed primarily for inference, with a GPU at it's core instead of a CPU.

Spread the 100 GW in our example across 1 billion homes and it comes to 100 watts per home, about as much as an old incandescent light bulb. The wiring, the outlet and the connection to the grid are already there which makes installing the machine trivial.

We still need to generate that electricity. But we can deliver it through connections that already serve those homes, without waiting to bring enormous amounts of power to a few new sites. Each computer can start working as soon as it arrives.

Precedents

History teaches us more about the future than any extrapolation can

The Mainframe

In 1970, sharing a computer made sense. The machine was expensive, it needed specialist staff, and most users needed only a fraction of its capacity. A university or a company could own one computer and divide its time among many people.

The early personal computer looked like a poor substitute. It had far less computing power and memory, and much less software. If the question was how to replace a mainframe, buying one made little sense.

IBM had built its business selling computers to organizations. It introduced its mass-market PC in 1981, after Apple and other early manufacturers had begun selling their machines. IBM’s entry helped turn what many still regarded as a hobbyist’s toy into a business tool.22

A machine on your desk gave you all of its limited capacity, whenever you wanted it. You could spend an evening learning to program, revising a budget, or trying something that might not work, without paying for each hour of computer time.

Useful software made that freedom worth buying. In 1979, VisiCalc gave people a reason to purchase an Apple II just to run a spreadsheet. They could change an assumption in a budget, watch the totals recalculate, and try another. A computer became something a business owner could use directly in the course of an ordinary working day.22

Steve Jobs with the Macintosh, January 1984. Photo: Bernard Gotfryd, public domain.

People bought these machines while they were still weak by the standards of institutional computing. Being powerful enough for the owner’s work, and always available to do it, mattered more than matching the largest computer on the market. Mainframes continued serving large organizations while a new industry grew around people buying machines for themselves.

The Best Businesses Sell a Product They Don’t Own

, the world’s largest taxi company, owns no vehicles.Tom Goodwin, TechCrunch, 201523

Airbnb followed the same logic with accommodation. Drivers supply cars; hosts supply homes. These companies make that capacity easy to find, book and pay for. They can add supply by bringing in another driver or host, without buying the car or building the house themselves.

With personal AI, the user can supply both the computer and its electricity. The company supplies the agent: the software that understands what the user wants, works with their apps, and makes the machine useful.

An AI company that rents its GPUs still has to pay for more computation as its users do more with their agents. Running those agents on the users’ own machines changes who pays for that capacity.

We think the best AI companies will provide inference without owning or renting the GPUs.

Apple and Nvidia already show part of this model. Nvidia’s DGX Spark, which began shipping in October 2025, puts an AI computer on the customer’s desk.24 Apple sells devices that can run its models locally. The customer buys the hardware and supplies the electricity.

Apple’s approach also leaves room for the cloud. Tasks that need more computation can go to Private Cloud Compute. The point is to let the customer’s machine do the work it can, and use remote capacity where it earns its cost.

Hybrid Inference

We do not think everything moves local. We think most of it does, and that the cloud stays for the moments that need it, at a fraction of its current share. That is already how computing works, and nobody finds it strange.

Think about where the work happens over a day on a MacBook. Moving the mouse, scrolling a page, writing a document: all of it runs on the machine in front of you, and once you own the machine it costs nothing more. A few times an hour you reach past it. You type something into Google, and for a fraction of a second a datacenter throws thousands of machines at your question. You open a website, and a server sends you the page. You hit send, and a mail server carries the message. Then the work comes back to your desk. Nobody calls that a cloud computer or a local computer. It is both, in a proportion you never have to think about.

The chart draws that day as one line. The dashed line across the middle is the on-device threshold. Below it, the work can be done on your own machine. Above it, the work needs a server somewhere else. Most of the day sits below the line. The 3 spikes are the moments you reached for the cloud, and each one lasted a fraction of a second. Hover over a spike, or tap it, and the chart shades the part above the line and marks it with a dollar sign. That is the part somebody has to pay for, every time it happens. Everything below the line is already paid for.

Now draw the same day for AI as it is served today. Every request goes to a frontier model in a datacenter, so the whole line sits above the threshold. Reading your email, ordering lunch, drafting a reply: all of it runs in the cloud, and all of it is billed by the token. The hard problems are up there too, but they are a small part of the day. That is why we think tokens are being needlessly wasted. Not because the cloud is used, but because it is used for everything.

There is a better way, because not every moment needs a frontier model. Reading your email, writing a reply, cross-pollinating your contacts, remembering what you said last week: a local model does these as well as a frontier model does, on your own GPU, at no marginal cost. Switch the chart above to hybrid inference and the line drops below the threshold for the whole day. It crosses the line twice, once to analyze a blood report and once to solve a hard problem. Those are the moments a frontier model earns its price.

Inference settles into the shape computing already has. The agent that runs all day, reading your screen and your mail, runs on your own GPU, because that is where the context is and because the marginal token is free. The hard problem, the one that needs a frontier model and a minute of thought, crosses the line for a few seconds and comes back. The cloud does not disappear. Its share just drops from everything to a few spikes a day.

The Innovator’s Dilemma

If you were choosing a company to build a personal AI computer, Apple would be the obvious choice. It designs the chips, controls the operating system, and knows how to turn a complicated technology into something people want in their homes.

The difficulty begins with the App Store.

Apple has spent years helping developers build businesses around software. Making those apps more useful with AI fits comfortably into that business. Letting AI replace some of them is a more awkward proposition.

Consider something small: an app you bought to organize a project or keep track of expenses. You probably wanted a fraction of its features and had to learn where someone else decided to put them. If your agent can make the tool you actually need, there may be no reason to shop for an app at all. You describe what you want, try it, and ask for changes.

Other software will still be worth buying. Services will still need customers. But increasingly, your agent could choose and operate that software for you. The companies behind it would have to earn their place by being useful to your agent, with fewer opportunities to keep you inside their own interfaces.

This is the same trap Google fell into when deciding whether to launch a chatbot. Doing so would result in the cannibalization of its search business, which ended up happening anyway as it had to compete with ChatGPT.

Apple may decide that making a better computer is worth changing how software is sold. It has reinvented its products before. But it has an enormous existing business to bring through that transition.

We can start with the assumption that the agent will operate the computer. It should be able to use existing apps, work across them, and make its own tools where that serves you better.

But doing all of this takes a startup that is unafraid to push the boundaries and can also build a supply chain, create AI-first silicon, write an operating system meant for an agent, and rebuild the computing experience around intelligence.

We spent two years doing that, and we think thousands of others will follow suit in the next 5.
